title: Interview · System Design
description: Seven system-design interview scenarios paired with the transferable architecture answer and how each maps to my real systems.

cards.front: Design a multi-channel notification platform handling ~7M messages/day (email/SMS/push/postal) with a synchronous acknowledgment and asynchronous fan-out. Walk the architecture.
cards.general: Start by clarifying the channels, the split between a synchronous ack and asynchronous downstream processing, and the daily volume. Put a synchronous front door in front that returns an acknowledgment immediately and hands the request off to a durable queue, decoupling upstream callers from downstream work. Behind the queue, run independently scalable, fault-isolated consumer stages — packaging, delivery-window scheduling, provider integration — so one slow stage can't stall the others. Publish lifecycle events on a streaming bus so state can be tracked in near-real-time without coupling the stages together. Guarantee correctness with dead-letter queues, retry logic, and idempotency so transient failures never produce duplicate or lost sends. Model preferences per-client / per-template / per-user so routing and content rules are data-driven.
cards.specific: I built the USAA 7M-msg/day notification platform: synchronous front door → SQS → per-stage Lambda consumers → external providers, with Kafka lifecycle events (generation-started → packaged → sent → delivery-confirmed) publishing alongside for state tracking with no internal coupling. Per-stage Lambda isolation, delivery-window scheduling, and DLQ/retry/idempotency are the real design I own. My preference data model is per-client/per-template/per-user rules.
cards.hint: Front door acks fast; heavy work is async behind the queue.

cards.front: On that 7M-msg/day notification platform, what does the 10-20s p99 latency figure actually refer to, and when should you bring it up?
cards.general: Be precise about which latency a number describes. A high tail like a 10-20 second p99 is not the acknowledgment path — a well-designed front door acks in milliseconds. That figure is peak processing latency on the asynchronous pipeline, i.e. how long an event can take to work its way through the downstream stages under load. Stating this distinction unprompted signals scale discipline and prevents an interviewer from mistaking your ack path for being slow.
cards.specific: On my USAA platform, the 10-20s p99 is peak event-processing latency on the async pipeline, never the ack-path latency. I raise this correction unprompted the moment scale comes up — I don't wait to be asked.
cards.hint: p99 discipline: async processing latency, not ack latency — say it unprompted.

cards.front: Design an enterprise RAG system with an evaluation harness. How do you build it and how do you prove retrieval quality?
cards.general: Clarify the corpus type, freshness requirements, and whether grounding/citation is mandatory. The pipeline is ingestion → chunking → embeddings → vector store → retrieval → grounded generation → citation. In the deep dive, discuss chunking-strategy trade-offs (size and overlap), embedding-model choice, and retrieval backends such as pgvector or Chroma. Prove quality with an eval harness measuring recall@k and MRR over a held-out QA set — that held-out set is the data model that makes the harness meaningful. Grounding and citation are the primary hallucination-mitigation mechanism; also design abstain behavior and watch for retrieval-quality regressions as failure modes.
cards.specific: My Policy RAG (USAA) is the full pipeline — chunking, HF embeddings, pgvector, LLM-grounded answers with citation, Terraform-provisioned infra — and its recall@k/MRR harness over a held-out QA set is the ONLY true-today eval-harness proof point in my portfolio. My FedInsight (public) project shows the ingestion craft: scraper → PyMuPDF column-aware parsing → 800/150-char overlap chunking → sentence-transformers embeddings → dual backends (pgvector + ChromaDB). Honesty caveat: I never claim FedInsight has its own eval numbers — that harness isn't built; my eval evidence is Policy RAG's.
cards.hint: recall@k / MRR on a held-out QA set is the eval evidence.

cards.front: Design an agentic assistant with guardrails — tool use and some autonomy. What's the architecture and how do you keep it safe?
cards.general: First clarify what 'agentic' means here: which tools, how much autonomy, and whether a human-in-the-loop is required. Architecturally, expose a typed tool catalogue (e.g. via MCP) and put an orchestration layer (e.g. LangGraph) on top. For richer tasks, a multi-agent topology helps: parallel researchers for coverage and redundancy, an analyst to reconcile, and a critic to check output quality, wired as a StateGraph fan-out/fan-in. Guardrails: sandboxed tools, SSRF protection on any web fetch, least-privilege scoping, and zero hard-coded secrets via runtime credential injection. Define the failure behavior explicitly — what happens when the critic rejects output — rather than guessing.
cards.specific: My FrostByte project contributes the typed @mcp.tool catalogue with zero-hardcoded-secret credential injection and a markdown-driven schema loader that grounds queries in real column definitions. My LocalLLM project contributes the multi-agent team topology: parallel researchers (I chose them for coverage/redundancy, not just speed) → analyst reconciles → critic checks quality, as a StateGraph fan-out/fan-in. Sandboxed file tools + SSRF-protected web search/fetch is the guardrail pattern spanning both. I state the true retry-vs-annotate behavior on critic rejection — I don't guess; my deep rehearsal lives in 05-localllm-deep-dive.md.
cards.hint: Typed MCP tools + orchestration; sandboxing, SSRF protection, no hard-coded secrets.

cards.front: Serve an LLM under tight cost constraints. How do you design the serving stack and the cost/latency levers?
cards.general: Clarify the latency budget, expected concurrency, and the VRAM/compute ceiling first. Serve a quantized model locally (e.g. via llama.cpp) behind a gateway, with provider fallback to a hosted API. In the deep dive, discuss the quantization trade-off (higher-precision quant for quality vs. a smaller one for VRAM-constrained hardware), an async concurrency queue, and a provider-abstraction switch that lets you retarget local vs. hosted. Keep provider selection in layered configuration so switching is a config change, not a code change. Failure modes: queue backpressure, and the cost/latency trade-off incurred when falling back to a hosted provider. This is a serving problem, not a training-at-scale problem.
cards.specific: My LocalLLM serves Gemma 4 12B via llama.cpp — Q6_K default, Q5_K profile for VRAM-constrained hardware. Its FastAPI OpenAI-compatible gateway means client code doesn't change when the backend does, and a protocol-based client SDK plus pydantic-settings layered config lets one switch retarget local ↔ OpenAI/Azure/Anthropic — the actual cost/latency lever. Honesty caveat: I never claim multi-node/distributed training experience here; this is serving, not training at scale (my honest deflection is in 08-mandatory-drills-and-weak-claims.md).
cards.hint: Quantized local serving behind an OpenAI-compatible gateway; config-switch fallback.

cards.front: Compare real-time transports — WebSocket vs. SSE vs. NDJSON/chunked-HTTP. When would you pick each?
cards.general: Clarify whether the need is bidirectional, one-way server push, or simple streaming. WebSocket is bidirectional and stateful — the right choice for interactive, two-way flows — but it needs explicit client reconnect logic and is the most likely to be blocked by corporate proxies/firewalls. SSE (text/event-stream) is one-way server push, the simplest option for token-by-token streaming, with browser-native reconnect and plain-HTTP robustness. NDJSON over chunked HTTP is the lightest infra footprint with no special protocol handling, read client-side via ReadableStream.getReader(), but has no built-in reconnect so the client must handle stream interruption. All three can sit on one backend. Failure modes: proxy/firewall friction on WebSocket, backpressure on SSE, and chunked-transfer edge cases on NDJSON.
cards.specific: All three are my LocalLLM claims on one FastAPI backend: WebSocket for live voice translation (VAD → ASR → MT → TTS, ≤8s lag) via @app.websocket + a React client; SSE for token-streamed completions on the OpenAI-compatible gateway; NDJSON over chunked HTTP for the web UI chat via ReadableStream. Attribution discipline: these are LocalLLM-ONLY — I never imply USAA's client-facing transport is WebSocket/SSE/NDJSON; that's unconfirmed and off-limits.
cards.hint: WebSocket = bidirectional/proxy-fragile; SSE = one-way/native reconnect; NDJSON = lightest/manual reconnect. LocalLLM-only.

cards.front: Firmwide/AIOps: design an anomaly-detection pipeline over operational telemetry. How do you ingest, detect, and gate remediation?
cards.general: Clarify the telemetry sources, what actually counts as an anomaly, and whether the scope is alerting or auto-remediation. Ingest lifecycle/telemetry events off a streaming bus into a warehouse for aggregation, then run a time-series anomaly/forecasting model on top. In the deep dive, cover schema design for multi-source telemetry, windowing/aggregation choices, and threshold-based vs. learned-baseline anomaly definitions — threshold is the simpler, honestly-scoped starting point and learned-baseline is the stretch. Reframe existing forecasting techniques as predictive health monitoring on a new signal. Critically, place a human-in-the-loop gate before any auto-remediation fires — as a design requirement, not an afterthought.
cards.specific: I reuse USAA's Kafka lifecycle events verbatim as the real, evidenced ingestion pattern → Snowflake ingestion/aggregation → time-series model — I don't invent a new telemetry pipeline. My FrostByte typed MCP access layer over Snowflake is the natural query/reporting layer on the warehouse. My EnergyBot forecasting techniques (regression, GBT, ARIMA-family, 3+ years production) are the honest technique transfer, reframed explicitly as 'predictive health monitoring' on operational metrics instead of demand data. Threshold-based detection is my honestly-scoped start; learned-baseline is my named stretch; a human-in-the-loop gate goes before any auto-remediation.
cards.hint: Kafka → Snowflake → EnergyBot forecasting, reframed; human gate before remediation.

cards.front: Firmwide/AIOps: design an agentic 'AIOps assistant' over MCP tools for a non-expert operator. How do you make tool exposure safe?
cards.general: Clarify who the non-expert user is and the blast radius of a wrong remediation action. Architecture: a conversational interface over a typed MCP tool catalogue with a ReAct-loop orchestration layer underneath. The security core is tool scoping and least privilege, with secure runtime credential injection rather than hard-coded secrets, plus sandboxed tools and SSRF protection. Model tools as schema definitions returning structured JSON. Guardrails against destructive unsupervised actions: no destructive action without explicit confirmation, and escalation to a human when confidence is low. Be honest about whether this is a shipped system or an extrapolation.
cards.specific: My FrostByte typed @mcp.tool catalogue + zero-hardcoded-secret credential injection is the direct precedent for safe tool exposure, and my LocalLLM LangGraph ReAct loop plus sandboxed-tool/SSRF-protection pattern generalizes to infra remediation tooling. Guardrails: least-privilege scoping, no destructive action without explicit confirmation, escalate to human on low confidence. Honesty caveat: this is my architectural extrapolation from FrostByte/LocalLLM, not a shipped AIOps system — I say so if pressed on whether it exists today.
cards.hint: Typed MCP tools + ReAct; least privilege, confirm before destructive, escalate on low confidence. Say it's extrapolation.
